claim: Transmissible cancers, in which cancer cells themselves act as an infectious agent, have been identified in Tasmanian devils, dogs, and four bivalves.
source: Transmissible cancers, in which cancer cells themselves act as an infectious agent, have been identified in Tasmanian devils, dogs, and four bivalves.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on transmissible cancers in these species.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia affecting M. chilensis in South America and M. edulis in Europe is a transmissible cancer.
source: We investigated a disseminated neoplasia affecting geographically distant populations of two species of mussels (Mytilus chilensis in South America and M. edulis in Europe). Sequencing alleles from four loci (two nuclear and two mitochondrial) provided evidence of transmissible cancer in both species.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from four genetic loci presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cancers in M. chilensis and M. edulis likely arose in M. trossulus.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of cancer-associated alleles and analysis of diagnostic SNPs showed that cancers in both species likely arose in a third species of mussel (M. trossulus), but these cancer cells are independent from the previously identified transmissible cancer in M. trossulus from Canada.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and SNP data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cancers in M. chilensis and M. edulis are independent from the previously identified transmissible cancer in M. trossulus from Canada (Mytilus BTN1).
source: Phylogenetic analysis of cancer-associated alleles and analysis of diagnostic SNPs showed that cancers in both species likely arose in a third species of mussel (M. trossulus), but these cancer cells are independent from the previously identified transmissible cancer in M. trossulus from Canada.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing distinct alleles from the Canadian BTN1 lineage.

claim: Cancers from M. chilensis and M. edulis are nearly identical, representing the same cancer lineage.
source: Unexpectedly, cancers from M. chilensis and M. edulis are nearly identical, showing that the same cancer lineage affects both.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data showing identical or nearly identical alleles at multiple loci.

claim: A single transmissible cancer lineage (Mytilus BTN2) has crossed into two new host species (M. chilensis and M. edulis).
source: Thus, a single transmissible cancer lineage has crossed into two new host species and has been transferred across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and between the Northern and Southern hemispheres.
evidence: This is supported by genetic data showing the same cancer lineage in both species across different geographic locations.

claim: The transmissible cancer lineage has been transferred across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and between the Northern and Southern hemispheres.
source: Thus, a single transmissible cancer lineage has crossed into two new host species and has been transferred across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and between the Northern and Southern hemispheres.
evidence: This is supported by the geographic distribution of samples showing the same cancer lineage in South America and Europe.

claim: Cancer cells can naturally transfer from one animal to another as an infectious allograft in Tasmanian devils, dogs, and bivalves.
source: In a few cases, however, including Tasmanian devils (Pearse and Swift, 2006; Pye et al., 2016), dogs (Murgia et al., 2006; Rebbeck et al., 2009), and bivalves (Metzger et al., 2016; Metzger et al., 2015), cancer cells naturally transfer from one animal to another as an infectious allograft, leading to lineages of transmissible cancer that spread through the populations (Metzger and Goff, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on transmissible cancers.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia in bivalves is a leukemia-like disease characterized by an amplification of rounded, polyploid cells in the hemolymph.
source: In bivalves, disseminated neoplasia (also called hemic neoplasia) is a leukemia-like disease that has been found in more than a dozen marine species, characterized by an amplification of rounded, polyploid cells in the hemolymph of animals that infiltrate into tissues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of disseminated neoplasia in bivalves.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia often occurs in outbreaks and has led to significant population losses in many bivalve species.
source: This disease often occurs in outbreaks and has led to significant population losses in many bivalve species (Barber, 2004; Carballal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on bivalve neoplasia.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia is a transmissible cancer in four bivalve species: soft-shell clams (Mya arenaria), cockles (Cerastoderma edule), golden carpet shell clams (Polititapes aureus), and bay mussels (Mytilus trossulus).
source: In four of the bivalve species affected by disseminated neoplasia (soft-shell clams, Mya arenaria; cockles, Cerastoderma edule; golden carpet shell clams, Polititapes aureus; and bay mussels, Mytilus trossulus), recent investigation has shown that the diseases are bivalve transmissible neoplasias (BTNs), showing that transmissible cancer may, in fact, be a common phenomenon in marine invertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research identifying these as transmissible cancers.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in marine mussels as early as 1969.
source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in marine mussels as early as 1969 (Farley, 1969), and has been observed consistently throughout Europe in both M. edulis (Green and Alderman, 1983; Lowe and Moore, 1978; Rasmussen, 1986) and M. galloprovincialis (Ciocan and Sunila, 2005; Carella et al., 2013; Gombač et al., 2013), albeit at lower prevalence than has been observed in some M. trossulus populations, which reached >20% in some locations in the 1980s and was associated with population losses (Barber, 2004; Bower et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Farley, 1969.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia has been observed consistently throughout Europe in both M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis.
source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in marine mussels as early as 1969 (Farley, 1969), and has been observed consistently throughout Europe in both M. edulis (Green and Alderman, 1983; Lowe and Moore, 1978; Rasmussen, 1986) and M. galloprovincialis (Ciocan and Sunila, 2005; Carella et al., 2013; Gombač et al., 2013), albeit at lower prevalence than has been observed in some M. trossulus populations, which reached >20% in some locations in the 1980s and was associated with population losses (Barber, 2004; Bower et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia prevalence in M. trossulus reached >20% in some locations in the 1980s and was associated with population losses.
source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in marine mussels as early as 1969 (Farley, 1969), and has been observed consistently throughout Europe in both M. edulis (Green and Alderman, 1983; Lowe and Moore, 1978; Rasmussen, 1986) and M. galloprovincialis (Ciocan and Sunila, 2005; Carella et al., 2013; Gombač et al., 2013), albeit at lower prevalence than has been observed in some M. trossulus populations, which reached >20% in some locations in the 1980s and was associated with population losses (Barber, 2004; Bower et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barber, 2004 and Bower et al., 1994.

claim: Mussels in the genus Mytilus form a complex of species including M. trossulus, M. edulis, M. galloprovincialis (native to the northern hemisphere) and M. chilensis, M. platensis, and M. planulatus (native to the southern hemisphere).
source: Mussels in the genus Mytilus form a complex of species, including M. trossulus, M. edulis, and M. galloprovincialis, native to the northern hemisphere, and M. chilensis, M. platensis, and M. planulatus, native to the southern hemisphere (Zbawicka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zbawicka et al., 2018.

claim: Mytilus species have an anti-tropical distribution, spanning the temperate waters of the world.
source: These species have an anti-tropical distribution, spanning the temperate waters of the world, and they can hybridize, leading to widespread introgression of allospecific alleles (Fraïsse et al., 2016) as well as hybrid zones in several locations (Bierne et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on Mytilus distribution.

claim: Mytilus species can hybridize, leading to widespread introgression of allospecific alleles and hybrid zones in several locations.
source: These species have an anti-tropical distribution, spanning the temperate waters of the world, and they can hybridize, leading to widespread introgression of allospecific alleles (Fraïsse et al., 2016) as well as hybrid zones in several locations (Bierne et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fraïsse et al., 2016 and Bierne et al., 2003.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in four Mytilus species across multiple continents.
source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in four of these Mytilus species across multiple continents (Barber, 2004; Carballal et al., 2015), but so far the only lineage of disseminated neoplasia in the genus that has been directly confirmed to be a transmissible cancer is in M. trossulus along the Pacific coast of British Columbia (BC), Canada (Metzger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The only lineage of disseminated neoplasia in the genus Mytilus that has been directly confirmed to be a transmissible cancer prior to this study is in M. trossulus along the Pacific coast of British Columbia, Canada.
source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in four of these Mytilus species across multiple continents (Barber, 2004; Carballal et al., 2015), but so far the only lineage of disseminated neoplasia in the genus that has been directly confirmed to be a transmissible cancer is in M. trossulus along the Pacific coast of British Columbia (BC), Canada (Metzger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Metzger et al., 2016.

claim: A population genetics analysis of M. edulis from France identified individuals with unexpected 'chimeric' signals containing M. trossulus alleles in a population where that species was absent.
source: A population genetics analysis of M. edulis from France, conducted to detect hybridization and introgression between Mytilus species by detecting species-specific SNPs, identified a few individuals with unexpected 'chimeric' signals. The DNA samples from these individuals included M. trossulus alleles in a population where that species was absent, and the ratio of the M. edulis and M. trossulus alleles were not consistent with a diploid hybrid genome. Instead, this could be better explained by a mixture of two genotypes (one M. edulis and one M. trossulus in origin) within a single individual (Riquet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Riquet et al., 2017.

claim: The 'chimeric' signals in M. edulis from France could be better explained by a mixture of two genotypes (one M. edulis and one M. trossulus in origin) within a single individual rather than a diploid hybrid genome.
source: The DNA samples from these individuals included M. trossulus alleles in a population where that species was absent, and the ratio of the M. edulis and M. trossulus alleles were not consistent with a diploid hybrid genome. Instead, this could be better explained by a mixture of two genotypes (one M. edulis and one M. trossulus in origin) within a single individual (Riquet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Riquet et al., 2017 and represents an inference from genetic data.

claim: A severe mass mortality event in French mussels began in 2014.
source: More recently, analysis of a severe mass mortality event (Benabdelmouna and Ledu, 2016) in French mussels that began in 2014 led to the observation of disseminated neoplasia in many populations of M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis (Benadelmouna et al., 2018), although it has not yet been determined whether this neoplasia is transmissible.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benabdelmouna and Ledu, 2016.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia was observed in many populations of M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis following a mass mortality event in French mussels.
source: More recently, analysis of a severe mass mortality event (Benabdelmouna and Ledu, 2016) in French mussels that began in 2014 led to the observation of disseminated neoplasia in many populations of M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis (Benadelmouna et al., 2018), although it has not yet been determined whether this neoplasia is transmissible.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benadelmouna et al., 2018.

claim: M. chilensis mussels are found along the western coast of South America.
source: M. chilensis mussels are found along the western coast of South America, and disseminated neoplasia has been reported in multiple populations in Chile and Argentina since 1998 (Lohrmann et al., 2019; Cremonte et al., 2015; Campalans et al., 1998; Cremonte et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of M. chilensis distribution.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in multiple populations of M. chilensis in Chile and Argentina since 1998.
source: M. chilensis mussels are found along the western coast of South America, and disseminated neoplasia has been reported in multiple populations in Chile and Argentina since 1998 (Lohrmann et al., 2019; Cremonte et al., 2015; Campalans et al., 1998; Cremonte et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia prevalence in M. chilensis has varied by location, ranging from undetectable in some populations to as high as 12% in the Castro region of Chile and 13% in the Beagle Channel in southern Argentina.
source: Prevalence has varied by location, ranging from undetectable in some populations to as high as 12% in the Castro region of Chile and 13% in the Beagle Channel in southern Argentina, although no notable mass mortality events have been associated with neoplasia in these populations.
evidence: This is based on data from the study or prior observations.

claim: No notable mass mortality events have been associated with neoplasia in M. chilensis populations.
source: Prevalence has varied by location, ranging from undetectable in some populations to as high as 12% in the Castro region of Chile and 13% in the Beagle Channel in southern Argentina, although no notable mass mortality events have been associated with neoplasia in these populations.
evidence: This is based on observations from the study or prior research.

claim: Mytilus BTN1 was able to be distinguished from normal M. trossulus genotypes at both a nuclear and mitochondrial locus.
source: Mytilus BTN1 was able to be distinguished from normal M. trossulus genotypes at both a nuclear and mitochondrial locus (Metzger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Metzger et al., 2016.

claim: 60 M. chilensis animals were collected from Argentina in 2012 with a disease prevalence of 10%.
source: To determine whether the disseminated neoplasia in M. chilensis was due to a conventional cancer or a transmissible cancer lineage, we collected 60 M. chilensis animals from Argentina in 2012. Histological analysis was used to diagnose the animals for the presence of disseminated neoplasia, and we observed a disease prevalence of 10%.
evidence: This is based on data from the study.

claim: Two of three diseased M. chilensis animals (Mch41 and Mch42) had four distinct EF1α alleles, consistent with a mixture of two host alleles and two cancer-specific alleles.
source: All three normal animals had one or two alleles, as expected, but two of the diseased animals (Mch41 and Mch42) had four distinct alleles, consistent with a mixture of two host alleles and two cancer-specific alleles (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two alleles (G and H) from diseased M. chilensis animal Mch41 were nearly exact matches to two alleles from Mch42, consistent with the presence of a transmissible cancer.
source: Notably, each diseased sample had two alleles that were unique (corresponding to host alleles), but two alleles from animal Mch41 were nearly exact matches to two alleles from Mch42 (here notated as G and H). This is consistent with the presence of a transmissible cancer containing alleles G and H.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and represents an inference about transmissible cancer.

claim: EF1α alleles cloned from a diseased M. chilensis individual from Chile exactly match the G and H cancer-associated sequences from Argentina.
source: A second collection of farmed M. chilensis from two locations in Chile confirmed the presence of disseminated neoplasia in these populations (9.6% in Calbuco and 4.5% in Castro). EF1α alleles cloned from a diseased individual from this location exactly match the G and H cancer-associated sequences from Argentina.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data from the study.

claim: Disseminated neoplasia prevalence in farmed M. chilensis from Chile was 9.6% in Calbuco and 4.5% in Castro.
source: A second collection of farmed M. chilensis from two locations in Chile confirmed the presence of disseminated neoplasia in these populations (9.6% in Calbuco and 4.5% in Castro).
evidence: This is based on data from the study.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis shows that the cancer-associated EF1α alleles (G and H) are likely of M. trossulus or M. chilensis origin.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of these putative cancer-associated alleles shows that they are likely of M. trossulus or M. chilensis origin (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both cancer-associated EF1α alleles (G and H) are clearly distinct from normal M. trossulus individuals and distinct from either allele of Mytilus BTN1.
source: However, both cancer-associated alleles are clearly distinct from normal M. trossulus individuals and distinct from either allele of the previously identified BC transmissible neoplasia, Mytilus BTN1.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The EF1α S allele from Mytilus BTN1 is closely related to a subset of normal M. trossulus alleles.
source: Additionally, phylogenetic analysis shows that the EF1α S allele from Mytilus BTN1 (previously termed the 'minor' allele) is closely related to a subset of normal M. trossulus alleles.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The phylogenetic tree is incompatible with the cancer-associated G and H alleles arising from the same cancer lineage as the Mytilus BTN1 S allele.
source: Thus, the tree is incompatible with the cancer-associated G and H alleles arising from the same cancer lineage as the Mytilus BTN1 S allele, although analysis of additional loci is needed to confirm this finding.
evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The BTN found in M. chilensis likely represents a separate, independent lineage of transmissible cancer, called Mytilus BTN2.
source: The BTN found in M. chilensis therefore likely represents a separate, independent lineage of transmissible cancer, here called Mytilus BTN2.
evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic and genetic data.

claim: More than the normal two EF1α alleles were found in three of four 'chimeric' M. edulis samples from the Atlantic coast of Europe.
source: We sequenced the EF1α alleles present in DNA from four of these 'chimeric' samples of M. edulis collected from locations on the Atlantic coast of Europe and found more than the normal two alleles in three of them (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Only one or two EF1α alleles were observed in normal M. edulis from the same populations.
source: Only one or two alleles were observed in normal M. edulis from the same populations.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claim: Two cancer-associated EF1α alleles found in diseased M. edulis exactly matched those found in cancer samples from M. chilensis in South America (Mytilus BTN2).
source: Unexpectedly, these two cancer-associated alleles found in diseased M. edulis did not match the previously reported Mytilus BTN1 lineage, found in M. trossulus in Canada, but instead exactly matched those found in cancer samples from M. chilensis in South America (Mytilus BTN2) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In European M. edulis cancer samples, alleles identical to the G allele from M. chilensis and two nearly identical versions of the H allele (H and H') were found.
source: In these European M. edulis cancer samples, we found alleles identical to the G allele from M. chilensis and two nearly identical versions of the H allele, with only one SNP between them (termed H').
evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claim: The H' allele likely represents a true second copy of the H allele within the cancer cells, consistent with a de novo mutation which occurred in one copy of the H allele after genome duplication.
source: Both the H and H' alleles were represented by multiple clones and found in multiple individuals, so H' likely represents a true second copy of the H allele within the cancer cells. Disseminated neoplasia is polyploid, and this result is consistent with a de novo mutation which occurred in one copy of the H allele after genome duplication (and likely after divergence of the South American and European strains of this lineage).
evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data and knowledge of polyploidy in disseminated neoplasia.

claim: 2-5 H4 alleles were observed in diseased M. chilensis and M. edulis samples and only 1-2 in normal samples.
source: We observed 2–5 alleles in diseased samples and only 1–2 in normal samples (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Looking only at normal H4 alleles, there is a clear grouping based on species of origin in a phylogenetic tree.
source: Looking only at normal alleles, there is a clear grouping based on species of origin in a phylogenetic tree (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Two sets of cancer-associated H4 alleles were identified from both M. chilensis and M. edulis, which group together.
source: Two sets of cancer-associated alleles were identified from both M. chilensis and M. edulis, which group together.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The H4 alleles associated with cancer in M. chilensis and M. edulis are distinct from the sequences of Mytilus BTN1 found in M. trossulus from Canada.
source: As with EF1α, the alleles associated with cancer in M. chilensis and M. edulis are distinct from the sequences of Mytilus BTN1 found in M. trossulus from Canada.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: There are H4 alleles found in normal M. trossulus individuals that are exact matches to alleles found in both Mytilus BTN1 and Mytilus BTN2.
source: Notably, there are alleles found in normal M. trossulus individuals that are exact matches to alleles found in both Mytilus BTN1 and Mytilus BTN2.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claim: Mytilus BTN1 likely arose within an M. trossulus individual with a 2A H4 allele and Mytilus BTN2 arose from a different M. trossulus individual which carried both MR-like and KNS-like alleles.
source: Mytilus BTN1 likely arose within an M. trossulus individual with a 2A H4 allele and Mytilus BTN2 arose from a different M. trossulus individual which carried both MR-like and KNS-like alleles.
evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic and sequencing data.

claim: Mytilus mussels have double uniparental inheritance of mitochondria, in which all individuals inherit mitochondria maternally, but a second male-specific lineage of mitochondria is also passed down to male offspring gonads.
source: As Mytilus mussels have double uniparental inheritance of mitochondria (in which all individuals inherit mitochondria maternally, but a second male-specific lineage of mitochondria is also passed down to male offspring gonads), we amplified a female allele from all individuals, and both female and male alleles from about half of the individuals (10 of 21 total) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Mytilus mitochondrial inheritance.

claim: A M. trossulus-like mitochondrial control region allele (termed 'D') was amplified from cancer samples from both M. edulis and M. chilensis.
source: In addition, we amplified a M. trossulus-like allele from cancer samples from both M. edulis and M. chilensis. This allele (termed 'D') is mostly female-like, but it switches to male-like sequence at the 3' end (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The D mitochondrial control region allele is mostly female-like, but it switches to male-like sequence at the 3' end.
source: This allele (termed 'D') is mostly female-like, but it switches to male-like sequence at the 3' end (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The D mitochondrial control region recombinant sequence closely matches a recombinant sequence previously reported in a Baltic M. trossulus individual.
source: This recombinant sequence closely matches a recombinant sequence previously reported in a Baltic M. trossulus individual (Śmietanka and Burzyński, 2017; Zbawicka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A second M. trossulus-like mitochondrial control region allele (C) was found in all three cancer samples of M. chilensis, which represents a recombination between female and male sequences with a different recombination point than the D allele.
source: Interestingly, a second M. trossulus-like allele (C) was found in all three cancer samples of M. chilensis, which also represents a recombination between female and male sequences, but with a different recombination point than the first.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claim: The presence of two recombinant mitochondrial control region alleles (C and D) argues for heteroplasmy of the cancer cells in M. chilensis.
source: This argues for heteroplasmy of the cancer cells in M. chilensis, and either loss of this heteroplasmy in the cancer lineage infecting M. edulis or capture of this new mitochondrial genome in the cancer lineage infecting M. chilensis.
evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data.

claim: The unique recombinant mitochondrial control region alleles argue that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 represent distinct lineages of cancer.
source: These unique recombinants between female and male sequences again argue that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 represent distinct lineages of cancer.
evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data.

claim: Both mitochondrial control region alleles (C and D) are distinct from those found in normal animals and from the previously identified Mytilus BTN1 lineage.
source: Even when considering only the region without any recombination with the male sequence (Figure 3C), both of these mitochondrial alleles are distinct from those found in normal animals and from the previously identified Mytilus BTN1 lineage, and the phylogenetic tree suggests that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 arose from different M. trossulus individuals.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The phylogenetic tree of mitochondrial control region alleles suggests that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 arose from different M. trossulus individuals.
source: Even when considering only the region without any recombination with the male sequence (Figure 3C), both of these mitochondrial alleles are distinct from those found in normal animals and from the previously identified Mytilus BTN1 lineage, and the phylogenetic tree suggests that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 arose from different M. trossulus individuals.
evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Standard 'universal' molluscan primers used for barcoding did not amplify the mtCOI allele from Mytilus BTN2.
source: Standard 'universal' molluscan primers used for barcoding (Folmer et al., 1994) did not amplify the mtCOI allele from Mytilus BTN2, but by using degenerate primers flanking the region, we were able to amplify and sequence mtCOI from all samples (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: A clear separation of the mtCOI mitogenomes of all three Mytilus species was identified, with the mtCOI from both Mytilus BTN1 and 2 nested within the M. trossulus sequences.
source: We identified a clear separation of the mitogenomes of all three species, with the mtCOI from both Mytilus BTN1 and 2 nested within the M. trossulus sequences, as with the three other loci tested (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Mytilus BTN1 mtCOI allele (U) showed clear differences from the Mytilus BTN2 allele (B).
source: The Mytilus BTN1 allele (U) again showed clear differences from the Mytilus BTN2 allele (B).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claim: The closest published mtCOI sequence to the Mytilus BTN2 allele is the sequence from 62mc10, a normal M. trossulus from the Baltic region.
source: As in the mitochondrial control region, the closest published sequence to the Mytilus BTN2 allele is the sequence from 62mc10, a normal M. trossulus from the Baltic region.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published sequences.

claim: The mtCOI data provide evidence that the two lineages of transmissible cancer (Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2) arose from distinct M. trossulus individuals.
source: This again provides evidence that the two lineages of transmissible cancer arose from distinct M. trossulus individuals.
evidence: This is an inference from sequencing and phylogenetic data.

claim: While the B mtCOI allele was found in Mytilus BTN2 samples from both Europe and Argentina, it was not identified in the M. chilensis samples from Chile.
source: Unexpectedly, while the B allele was found in Mytilus BTN2 samples from both Europe and Argentina, it was not identified in the M. chilensis samples from Chile.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claim: The Chilean M. chilensis samples show evidence of the common Mytilus BTN2 alleles at all other nuclear and mitochondrial loci, suggesting recombination between cancer and host mitochondria.
source: These samples show evidence of the common Mytilus BTN2 alleles at all other nuclear and mitochondrial loci, so this suggests that there has been recombination between cancer and host mitochondria somewhere in the M. chilensis population, resulting in a subset of Mytilus BTN2 cells in Chile with new recombinant mitogenomes.
evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data.

claim: qPCR showed that the cancer-associated EF1α allele was found in all three M. chilensis samples from Argentina that were diagnosed as diseased, including Mch23.
source: Analysis of the M. chilensis samples showed that the cancer-associated allele was found in all three samples from Argentina that were diagnosed as diseased, including Mch23 (Figure 5), and it was undetectable in all three normal samples.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The cancer-associated EF1α allele was undetectable in all three normal M. chilensis samples from Argentina by qPCR.
source: Analysis of the M. chilensis samples showed that the cancer-associated allele was found in all three samples from Argentina that were diagnosed as diseased, including Mch23 (Figure 5), and it was undetectable in all three normal samples.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean, two of the four diseased animals had high levels of the cancer-associated EF1α allele, but the other two did not.
source: In the M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean, however, we found that two of the four diseased animals had high levels of the cancer-associated allele, but the other two did not. They likely have either conventional cancer or a different transmissible cancer lineage.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claim: Two diseased M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean likely have either conventional cancer or a different transmissible cancer lineage.
source: In the M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean, however, we found that two of the four diseased animals had high levels of the cancer-associated allele, but the other two did not. They likely have either conventional cancer or a different transmissible cancer lineage.
evidence: This is an inference from qPCR data.

claim: qPCR showed the presence of the cancer-associated EF1α allele in all M. edulis mussels diagnosed as diseased but not in normal samples.
source: In M. edulis, qPCR showed the presence of the cancer-associated allele in all mussels diagnosed as diseased but not in normal samples.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claim: The allele associated with Mytilus BTN2 in M. edulis and M. chilensis was undetectable in both normal and diseased M. trossulus samples from Canada by qPCR.
source: To test whether Mytilus BTN2 could be present in the Canadian individuals at a low level, qPCR analysis was conducted on the original samples from which Mytilus BTN1 was identified (Metzger et al., 2016). The allele associated with Mytilus BTN2 in M. edulis and M. chilensis was undetectable in both normal and diseased M. trossulus samples from Canada.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claim: Both cancer-associated H4 alleles were detected by qPCR in all animals diagnosed as diseased except for the two Chilean samples that were negative for the cancer-associated EF1α allele.
source: qPCR primers specific for both cancer-associated H4 alleles were made, and both were detected in all animals diagnosed as diseased except for the two Chilean samples that were negative for the cancer-associated EF1α allele (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: One H4 cancer-associated allele was present at a higher level within each diseased animal than the other, but the ratio of the two alleles was not completely consistent across all individuals.
source: One allele was present at a higher level within each diseased animal than the other, but the ratio of the two alleles was not completely consistent across all individuals, suggesting that there has been recombination or copy number variation in some subgroups of the cancer lineage.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data and represents an inference about recombination or copy number variation.

claim: The H4 cancer-associated alleles were identified in several normal M. trossulus by qPCR.
source: The H4 cancer-associated alleles were also identified in several normal M. trossulus. This confirms that H4 alleles found in Mytilus BTN2 are present in some individuals in the normal M. trossulus population.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claim: H4 alleles found in Mytilus BTN2 are present in some individuals in the normal M. trossulus population.
source: The H4 cancer-associated alleles were also identified in several normal M. trossulus. This confirms that H4 alleles found in Mytilus BTN2 are present in some individuals in the normal M. trossulus population. This is expected, as each of the two transmissible cancer lineages arose in the past from a different normal M. trossulus individual.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data and represents an expected finding given the origin of the cancer.

claim: The C mitochondrial control region allele is present in M. chilensis cancers at a very low level (<1% of total allele fraction).
source: Analysis of the two cancer-associated mitochondrial control region alleles shows that the C allele (only cloned from M. chilensis samples) is present in M. chilensis cancers at a very low level (<1% of total allele fraction).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claim: The C mitochondrial control region allele was undetectable in four of eight diseased M. edulis, suggesting that this heteroplasmy may be lost in some of the cancer cells spreading in the M. edulis population.
source: It was also undetectable in four of eight diseased M. edulis, again suggesting that this heteroplasmy may be lost in some of the cancer cells spreading in the M. edulis population (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5 and represents an inference about heteroplasmy loss.

claim: The D mitochondrial control region allele contains a tandem repeat with multiple copies of the control region.
source: Unexpectedly, when comparing the copy number of the D allele to amplification at a conserved locus about 200 bp away (shown schematically in Figure 3B), the neoplastic samples yielded values greater than 100%. Further investigation revealed a tandem repeat in the D mitochondrial genome, with multiple copies of the control region that are targeted by allele-specific primers. A tandem repeat was confirmed by generating the reverse complement of the qPCR primers specific for allele D and amplifying and sequencing the tandem repeat junction (marked in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on qPCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Analysis of the mtCOI locus by qPCR confirmed that the main Mytilus BTN2 allele was identified in all M. edulis cancer samples, and in the Argentinian M. chilensis, but not the Chilean M. chilensis.
source: Analysis of the mtCOI locus by qPCR confirmed that the main Mytilus BTN2 allele was identified in all M. edulis cancer samples, and in the Argentinian M. chilensis, but not the Chilean M. chilensis.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claim: The mitochondria in the Chilean M. chilensis samples (Castro26 and 52) has been completely replaced with one that is a recombinant of the original Mytilus BTN2 M. trossulus-derived sequence and newly acquired M. chilensis-derived sequence.
source: This suggests that the mitochondria in the Chilean samples (Castro26 and 52) has been completely replaced with one that is a recombinant of the original Mytilus BTN2 M. trossulus-derived sequence and newly acquired M. chilensis-derived sequence.
evidence: This is an inference from qPCR and sequencing data.

claim: Two samples from Chile (Castro49 and 84) do not have the Mytilus BTN2 cancer lineage.
source: Analyses at all loci confirm that two samples from Chile (Castro49 and 84) are not afflicted by Mytilus BTN2, while it is present at high levels in the other two diseased samples from Chile and all three tested samples from Argentina and eight from Europe. These two animals without any of the Mytilus BTN2 markers at any of the four loci thus do not have the Mytilus BTN2 cancer lineage.
evidence: This is based on analysis of multiple loci by qPCR and sequencing.

claim: The EF1α qPCR assay is the most highly sensitive and specific assay for detecting Mytilus BTN2 within these populations.
source: Overall, the EF1α qPCR assay is the most highly sensitive and specific assay within these populations, with detection of the cancer-associated allele in all samples known to be affected by Mytilus BTN2 and no detectible amplification in any normal samples.
evidence: This is based on comparison of qPCR assay performance across multiple loci.

claim: All six Mytilus BTN2-positive M. edulis and all three positive M. chilensis have strong fluorescence corresponding to the M. trossulus allele at all diagnostic SNP loci analyzed.
source: We confirm that all six Mytilus BTN2-positive M. edulis and all three positive M. chilensis analysed with the SNP assay have strong fluorescence corresponding to the M. trossulus allele at all diagnostic loci analysed and they are clear outliers in the compound multi-locus average (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on SNP assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: No normal animals of either M. edulis or M. chilensis have a signal of an M. trossulus allele at more than one SNP locus.
source: In contrast, no normal animals of either species have a signal of an M. trossulus allele at more than one locus.
evidence: This is based on SNP assay data from the study.

claim: Data from multiple independent SNP loci provide evidence supporting the finding that the Mytilus BTN2 lineage is an M. trossulus derived cancer.
source: Therefore, data from multiple independent loci provide further evidence supporting the finding that the Mytilus BTN2 lineage is an M. trossulus derived cancer.
evidence: This is based on SNP assay data and represents an inference about the origin of the cancer.

claim: The finding of a single cancer lineage crossing into multiple species across vast distances is unexpected.
source: Disseminated neoplasia has been previously shown to be due to a transmissible cancer lineage in four bivalve species, including Mytilus trossulus (Metzger et al., 2016; Metzger et al., 2015), and the current study greatly extends both our understanding of cross-species transmission of cancer (from M. trossulus into two other Mytilus species) and our understanding of the potential for geographic spread of transmissible cancers (Figure 7). This finding of a single lineage crossing into multiple species across such vast distances is unexpected.
evidence: This is a statement of interpretation of the findings.

claim: Phylogenetic evidence from four loci and SNP data from 13 diagnostic nuclear SNPs show that Mytilus BTN2 is distinct from Mytilus BTN1.
source: Phylogenetic evidence from four loci and SNP data from 13 diagnostic nuclear SNPs show that the lineage identified here (Mytilus BTN2) is distinct from Mytilus BTN1, and that it too arose from a M. trossulus individual before crossing into other Mytilus species, as previously proposed (Riquet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and SNP data from the study.

claim: Mytilus BTN2 arose from a M. trossulus individual before crossing into other Mytilus species.
source: Phylogenetic evidence from four loci and SNP data from 13 diagnostic nuclear SNPs show that the lineage identified here (Mytilus BTN2) is distinct from Mytilus BTN1, and that it too arose from a M. trossulus individual before crossing into other Mytilus species, as previously proposed (Riquet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and SNP data from the study and represents an inference about the origin of the cancer.

claim: The gene trees of the four loci are all concordant with each other and consistent with a clonal, asexual cancer lineage derived from an M. trossulus cancer that is independent from Mytilus BTN1.
source: The gene trees of the four loci are all concordant with each other, and are all consistent with a clonal, asexual cancer lineage derived from an M. trossulus cancer that is independent from Mytilus BTN1.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of multiple loci.

claim: The only exception to the concordance of gene trees is the observation of recombination with host mitochondrial DNA in the mitogenomes of Mytilus BTN2 in Chile.
source: The only exception to this is the observation of recombination with host mitochondrial DNA in the mitogenomes of Mytilus BTN2 in Chile.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data showing recombinant mitochondrial sequences.

claim: The age of the Mytilus BTN2 cancer lineage is unknown.
source: The age of this cancer lineage is unknown, but the other transmissible cancer with world-wide spread (canine transmissible venereal tumor; CTVT) was estimated to be thousands of years old (Murchison et al., 2014; Baez-Ortega et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the age of the cancer.

claim: Canine transmissible venereal tumor (CTVT) was estimated to be thousands of years old.
source: The age of this cancer lineage is unknown, but the other transmissible cancer with world-wide spread (canine transmissible venereal tumor; CTVT) was estimated to be thousands of years old (Murchison et al., 2014; Baez-Ortega et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: If the earliest reports of disseminated neoplasia in M. edulis were attributable to Mytilus BTN2, it would be at least 50 years old.
source: Our oldest samples are 10 years old, but if the earliest reports of disseminated neoplasia in M. edulis were attributable to this same lineage (Farley, 1969), it would be at least 50 years old.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the earliest reports of disseminated neoplasia.

claim: The transmission of cancer cells from the Northern to the Southern Hemisphere and from Atlantic to Pacific Oceans is remarkable.
source: The transmission of cancer cells from the Northern to the Southern Hemisphere and from Atlantic to Pacific Oceans is remarkable, and ocean currents are unlikely to provide a mechanism for travel in either direction (especially given that anti-tropical distribution prevents a stepping-stone for trans-equatorial propagation).
evidence: This is a statement of interpretation of the findings.

claim: Ocean currents are unlikely to provide a mechanism for travel of cancer cells from the Northern to the Southern Hemisphere or from Atlantic to Pacific Oceans.
source: The transmission of cancer cells from the Northern to the Southern Hemisphere and from Atlantic to Pacific Oceans is remarkable, and ocean currents are unlikely to provide a mechanism for travel in either direction (especially given that anti-tropical distribution prevents a stepping-stone for trans-equatorial propagation).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of ocean currents and Mytilus distribution.

claim: The most likely route of transmission of Mytilus BTN2 is human intervention, specifically the transportation of animals harboring neoplastic cells in or on shipping vessels.
source: The most likely route of transmission is human intervention, specifically the transportation of animals harboring neoplastic cells in or on shipping vessels.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism of transmission.

claim: Examples of anthropogenic introduction of invasive species via shipping transport and aquaculture are common throughout the globe.
source: While it is difficult to experimentally prove that a particular disease transmission was due to accidental transport on shipping vessels, examples of anthropogenic introduction of invasive species via shipping transport and aquaculture are common throughout the globe (Molnar et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The accidental anthropogenic introduction of Mytilus species includes M. galloprovincialis introduced in northern Chile and Argentina, M. edulis introduced in BC and the Kerguelen Islands, and M. trossulus into Scotland.
source: The accidental anthropogenic introduction of Mytilus species includes M. galloprovincialis introduced in northern Chile (Daguin and Borsa, 2000) and Argentina (Zbawicka et al., 2018), M. edulis introduced in BC (Crego-Prieto et al., 2015) and the Kerguelen Islands (Fraisse et al., 2018), and M. trossulus into Scotland (Dias et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Since Mytilus species are known to adhere to ships and spread accidentally across the world, and transmissible cancer can have an incubation period of weeks to months, any diseased animal which adheres to a ship could lead to the spread of a transmissible cancer to new and potentially susceptible populations.
source: Since Mytilus species are known to adhere to ships and spread accidentally across the world, and transmissible cancer can have an incubation period of weeks to months, any diseased animal which adheres to a ship could lead to the spread of a transmissible cancer to new and potentially susceptible populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of Mytilus behavior and transmissible cancer incubation periods.

claim: If transmissible cancers are able to readily travel along shipping lines and infect closely related species, then this and other lineages of transmissible cancer have the potential for world-wide reach.
source: If transmissible cancers are able to readily travel along shipping lines and infect closely related species, then this and other lineages of transmissible cancer have the potential for world-wide reach.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential spread of transmissible cancers.

claim: The initial sequencing and amplification of the EF1α loci from M. edulis and M. chilensis samples were conducted by different people at different sites before any plasmids containing the sequence from one site had been transferred to the other.
source: In this case, the initial sequencing and amplification of the EF1α loci from M. edulis and M. chilensis samples were conducted by different people at different sites before any plasmids containing the sequence from one site had been transferred to the other.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedures used to prevent contamination.

claim: The EF1α qPCR assay was independently replicated on European M. edulis infected individuals in two labs, in USA and France.
source: The EF1α qPCR assay was independently replicated on European M. edulis infected individuals in two labs, in USA and France.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedures used to validate findings.

claim: The finding of slight differences between the two subgroups of Mytilus BTN2 cancer lineage argues against a single source of contamination.
source: Also, the finding of slight differences between the two subgroups of this cancer lineage argue against a single source of contamination.
evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data that argues against contamination.

claim: qPCR verification confirms that a significant fraction of the DNA of each diseased sample contains the cancer-associated allele, and that it is not found in DNA samples from normal animals.
source: Additionally, qPCR verification confirms that a significant fraction of the DNA of each sample contains the cancer-associated allele, and that it is not found in DNA samples from normal animals, which have been treated in the same way.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claim: The data could not be due to contamination with a small amount of DNA and represents genuine identification of a nearly identical cancer from mussels of different continents and species.
source: Therefore, the data could not be due to contamination with a small amount of DNA and represents genuine identification of a nearly identical cancer from mussels of different continents and species.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and procedures.

claim: Invertebrates do not possess a vertebrate-like adaptive immune system or a major histocompatibility complex.
source: Invertebrates do not possess a vertebrate-like adaptive immune system or a major histocompatibility complex, which vertebrates utilize for discriminating self from nonself.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of invertebrate immunology.

claim: In most previously identified cases of BTN, the neoplasia has only been identified in the species of origin.
source: However, in most previously identified cases of BTN, the neoplasia has only been identified in the species of origin (Metzger et al., 2016; Metzger et al., 2015), and attempts to experimentally transfer neoplastic cells from M. trossulus or the soft-shell clam Mya arenaria into several bivalve species have only been successful when the transfer is between members of the same species (Kent et al., 1991; Mateo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attempts to experimentally transfer neoplastic cells from M. trossulus or Mya arenaria into several bivalve species have only been successful when the transfer is between members of the same species.
source: However, in most previously identified cases of BTN, the neoplasia has only been identified in the species of origin (Metzger et al., 2016; Metzger et al., 2015), and attempts to experimentally transfer neoplastic cells from M. trossulus or the soft-shell clam Mya arenaria into several bivalve species have only been successful when the transfer is between members of the same species (Kent et al., 1991; Mateo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The species in the Mytilus complex are able to hybridize, so the barrier to cross-species transmission may be relatively low.
source: The species in the Mytilus complex are able to hybridize, so the barrier to cross-species transmission may be relatively low.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of Mytilus hybridization.

claim: The disseminated neoplasia found on the Pacific coast of North America (which was identified as originating from M. trossulus) was found in M. trossulus at a much higher prevalence than M. edulis in the same region.
source: However, it has been reported that the disseminated neoplasia found on the Pacific coast of North America (which was identified as originating from M. trossulus) was found in M. trossulus at a much higher prevalence than M. edulis in the same region (Muttray et al., 2007), which suggested that the M. trossulus cancer preferentially infected M. trossulus hosts.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muttray et al., 2007.

claim: It is currently unknown whether Mytilus BTN2 would be able to infect its original host species or if the original host has evolved resistance.
source: It is currently unknown whether Mytilus BTN2 would be able to infect its original host species or if the original host has evolved resistance, as was suggested with the cancer derived from the pullet shell clam Venerupis corrugata (Metzger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the host range of Mytilus BTN2.

claim: M. chilensis is closely related to M. edulis, and it has even been suggested that it could be considered a subspecies, M. edulis platensis.
source: M. chilensis is closely related to M. edulis, and it has even been suggested that it could be considered a subspecies, M. edulis platensis (Borsa et al., 2012), although this is controversial (Zbawicka et al., 2018), so once the cancer was able to cross into either M. chilensis or M. edulis, the second jump into the other species may have presented a lower barrier.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Once Mytilus BTN2 was able to cross into either M. chilensis or M. edulis, the second jump into the other species may have presented a lower barrier.
source: M. chilensis is closely related to M. edulis, and it has even been suggested that it could be considered a subspecies, M. edulis platensis (Borsa et al., 2012), although this is controversial (Zbawicka et al., 2018), so once the cancer was able to cross into either M. chilensis or M. edulis, the second jump into the other species may have presented a lower barrier.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the ease of cross-species transmission.

claim: Based on analysis of transmissible cancers in devils and dogs it has been hypothesized that transmissible cancers primarily occur in inbred populations.
source: Based on analysis of transmissible cancers in devils and dogs it has been hypothesized that transmissible cancers primarily occur in inbred populations, but the finding of this cancer spreading into highly outbred individuals from multiple different species within the same genus shows that this constraint is not universal.
evidence: This is based on prior hypotheses about transmissible cancers.

claim: The finding of Mytilus BTN2 spreading into highly outbred individuals from multiple different species within the same genus shows that the constraint of inbreeding for transmissible cancers is not universal.
source: Based on analysis of transmissible cancers in devils and dogs it has been hypothesized that transmissible cancers primarily occur in inbred populations, but the finding of this cancer spreading into highly outbred individuals from multiple different species within the same genus shows that this constraint is not universal.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of the study.

claim: The evidence for mitochondrial heteroplasmy and recombination observed in Mytilus BTN2 and its loss or gain suggests a dynamic mitochondrial population in BTN, which may not exactly match the nuclear evolutionary path.
source: The evidence for mitochondrial heteroplasmy and recombination observed in this cancer lineage and its loss or gain is a very interesting observation that suggests a dynamic mitochondrial population in BTN, which may not exactly match the nuclear evolutionary path.
evidence: This is an inference from the mitochondrial data.

claim: Mitochondria in CTVT has been replaced several times by mitochondrial capture of new normal mitochondrial genomes.
source: It has been shown that mitochondria in CTVT has been replaced several times by mitochondrial capture of new normal mitochondrial genomes (Rebbeck et al., 2011; Strakova et al., 2016), so a dynamic mitochondrial population may be a common feature among transmissible cancers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A dynamic mitochondrial population may be a common feature among transmissible cancers.
source: It has been shown that mitochondria in CTVT has been replaced several times by mitochondrial capture of new normal mitochondrial genomes (Rebbeck et al., 2011; Strakova et al., 2016), so a dynamic mitochondrial population may be a common feature among transmissible cancers.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on observations in CTVT and Mytilus BTN2.

claim: One of the two cancer-associated mtCR regions could be a nuclear-to-mitochondrial transfer (numt) of a copy of the control region instead of mitochondrial heteroplasmy.
source: It is also possible that one of the two cancer-associated mtCR regions could be a nuclear-to-mitochondrial transfer (numt) of a copy of the control region instead of mitochondrial heteroplasmy, as this possibility cannot be excluded by PCR of total extracted DNA.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the data.

claim: Mitochondrial replacement has not yet been described in any BTN.
source: Mitochondrial replacement has not yet been described in any BTN, so further analysis will be required to determine the full recombinant cancer mitogenomes and to test whether there is any selective advantage of this recombinant mitogenome in Mytilus BTN2.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding BTN mitochondrial replacement.

claim: Comparison of cancer-associated sequences to those found in normal M. trossulus populations may allow identification of the location of the origin of these cancer lineages.
source: Comparison of cancer-associated sequences to those found in normal M. trossulus populations may allow us to identify the location of the origin of these cancer lineages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future analysis.

claim: BLAST searches for the neoplasia-associated alleles most closely match M. trossulus from the Baltic and BC.
source: BLAST searches for the neoplasia-associated alleles most closely match M. trossulus from the Baltic and BC.
evidence: This is based on BLAST searches of sequence databases.

claim: The Mytilus BTN2 recombinant mitochondrial sequences closely match the recombinant sequence first identified in the Baltic (62mc10), but this haplotype is actually rare in the Baltic, with similar recombinant haplotypes more commonly found on the coast of Norway.
source: The Mytilus BTN2 recombinant mitochondrial sequences closely match the recombinant sequence first identified in the Baltic (62mc10), but this haplotype is actually rare in the Baltic, with similar recombinant haplotypes more commonly found on the coast of Norway (Śmietanka and Burzyński, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Śmietanka and Burzyński, 2017.

claim: Mytilus BTN2 likely originated in Northern Europe, but it may not necessarily be from the Baltic.
source: This suggests that this cancer lineage originated in Northern Europe, but it may not necessarily be from the Baltic.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on sequence similarity.

claim: The exact population of origin of Mytilus BTN2 remains uncertain.
source: Therefore, the exact population of origin of this cancer remains uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the origin of the cancer.

claim: Two lineages of cancer from two separate M. trossulus individuals have turned into BTN lineages.
source: Overall, these data show that two lineages of cancer from two separate M. trossulus individuals have turned into BTN lineages, and one of these lineages (Mytilus BTN2) has spread world-wide throughout multiple host species.
evidence: This is a summary inference from all the data presented.

claim: One of the BTN lineages (Mytilus BTN2) has spread world-wide throughout multiple host species.
source: Overall, these data show that two lineages of cancer from two separate M. trossulus individuals have turned into BTN lineages, and one of these lineages (Mytilus BTN2) has spread world-wide throughout multiple host species.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: The spread of Mytilus BTN2 suggests that anthropogenic influence may exacerbate the spread of cancers and may allow access into new environments and new populations, where the pathogenic potential is unknown.
source: This spread also suggests that anthropogenic influence may exacerbate the spread of cancers and may allow access into new environments and new populations, where the pathogenic potential is unknown.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the findings.
